summaries.gardner: Canadian Natural has the momentum Gardner likes (up about 74% in the 52 weeks to mid-October 2026) and a long record of disciplined management, but it is Canada's largest oil and gas producer in a mature commodity industry, not the top dog in an emerging one. Its advantage is low-cost, long-life reserves rather than a brand or innovation, so it fits few Rule Breaker traits.
summaries.buffett: The business is simple and owns hard-to-replicate assets (15.9 billion BOE of proved reserves, a 31-year proved reserve life) with low costs and 26 consecutive years of dividend growth, which Buffett would respect. But earnings swing with oil prices (a C$435M loss in 2020, C$10,937M profit in 2022) and at about 13.7 times trailing earnings and 3.4 times book value there is no clear margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would admire the owner-led, cost-obsessed culture under Executive Chair Murray Edwards and its low-decline assets that need little reinvestment to sustain output. Inverting, the main ways to lose are an oil-price collapse, carbon policy and pipeline access, and the long-term energy transition, though moderate debt makes outright failure unlikely.
summaries.lynch: Canadian Natural is a classic Lynch cyclical, and its 2026 earnings are lifted by a Middle East-driven oil spike (WTI US$92.85 in Q2 2026), when cyclicals often look cheapest. The share count is falling steadily (diluted shares from 2,363.5M in 2020 to 2,089.8M in Q2 2026, split-adjusted), but analysts expect adjusted EPS to drop about 10% in 2027.
summaries.fisher: It scores on Fisher's points for cost control, operating know-how and long-range planning (expansions such as the 150,000 bbl/d Jackpine mine), but it sells undifferentiated oil and gas with no special sales organisation or research-driven new products. Growth comes from acquisitions, debottlenecking and oil prices rather than innovation.
summaries.graham: It passes Graham's tests for size and dividend record (26 consecutive years of increases), but fails on earnings stability (a loss in 2020), on its current ratio of about 1.0, and on price: about 19.7 times three-year average earnings and a P/E times P/B of about 47.
summaries.thiel: Canadian Natural does not fit Thiel's monopoly view: it sells a commodity at world prices with no 10x proprietary technology. Its scarce oil sands reserves are a durable asset but not a technology-driven monopoly.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner favours secular growth compounders with clear catalysts; Canadian Natural's 2026 jump came mostly from higher oil prices, and its 2025 revenue of C$38,762M was below 2022's C$42,298M. It could fit a tactical energy view, not his long-duration growth style.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller trades macro themes and momentum, and CNQ has both in 2026: Middle East supply disruption lifted WTI to US$92.85 in Q2 2026 and the shares rose about 74% in a year. The thesis depends on oil prices staying high and on Canadian policy (Pathways, pipelines), so it fits as a macro trade rather than a long-term core holding.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith avoids cyclical, capital-heavy businesses without pricing power; Canadian Natural earns respectable returns (ROIC about 14%) from low-decline assets but its profits depend on oil prices it cannot set. It would not meet his definition of a good company.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula Canadian Natural looks reasonable: return on invested capital of about 14% and EV/EBIT of about 15-16, an operating earnings yield of roughly 6-7%. Those figures are middling rather than top-ranked and rest on elevated 2026 oil prices.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool needs a great business, great management and great reinvestment; Canadian Natural has proven, owner-minded management and some high-return debottlenecking projects, but the business is a commodity producer and most cash is paid out (about C$9.0 billion returned in 2025). It fits the management leg best.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai buys simple businesses during temporary distress at deep discounts; Canadian Natural was such a case in 2020, but in October 2026 it trades near its 52-week high after the oil spike. Long-life reserves and moderate debt limit permanent-loss risk, but the price is not a bargain.
summaries.wood: Canadian Natural is the opposite of ARK's disruptive-innovation themes; ARK expects electric vehicles and cheaper batteries to reduce oil demand over time. It has no meaningful exposure to AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomics.
summaries.ackman: Ackman wants simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with pricing power and low exposure to outside forces; Canadian Natural is simple and generates strong free cash flow (about C$9.7 billion over the last twelve months) but has no pricing power and depends on oil prices and Canadian policy. It does not fit his core criteria.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's scale-economics-shared model does not apply to a commodity producer selling at market prices. Canadian Natural's scale lowers its costs, but the savings are kept as margin and returned to shareholders rather than passed on to customers.
summaries.valentine: Valentine backed young companies attacking huge, fast-growing markets with products that solve painful problems; Canadian Natural supplies essential energy but in a mature market as a company incorporated in 1973. It is far from the kind of opportunity Sequoia looks for.
summaries.nash: Canadian Natural fails Tom Nash's process early: it is a commodity producer (a zone to avoid) and debt (C$17,144M) far exceeds cash (C$2,618M), although its operating margin of about 24% clears his 20% floor. Its 13-category score is about 65 of 130, the price implies about 16% annual revenue growth for five years against a three-year revenue CAGR of -2.9%, and his DCF gives roughly US$26 a share against US$54.12, so it fails his valuation steps too.

momentum.evidence: CNQ rose about 74% over the 52 weeks to October 16, 2026 (StockAnalysis), to US$54.12 on October 19 near its 52-week high of US$54.33, far ahead of the broad market.

g4.evidence: Management led by Executive Chair N. Murray Edwards (director since 1988, 42.9 million shares) and President Scott Stauth is highly regarded for capital discipline, but the stock is held mainly by institutions (about 81%) rather than famous concentrated investors.

g6.evidence: After the 2026 rally the price sits above the average analyst target of about US$48 (StockAnalysis), so some see it as fully valued, but a forward P/E of about 11.6 is not widely called overvalued.

simple.evidence: It produces and sells crude oil, synthetic crude and natural gas from Canadian oil sands and wells, a business a careful generalist can follow.

b2.evidence: Results swing with oil prices: a net loss of C$435M in 2020, profits of C$10,937M in 2022 and C$6,106M in 2024.

integrity.evidence: Management is owner-aligned (Edwards holds 42.9 million shares; executives must hold four times salary in shares), reports clearly against a published returns policy, and 10 of 12 directors are independent.

b6.evidence: Deals like Chevron's oil sands and Duvernay assets (US$6.5B, December 2024) and the AOSP swap fit its long-life strategy, but they also continue a long series of acquisitions that built its size.

roic.evidence: ROIC is about 14% and ROE about 27% on trailing figures (StockAnalysis), with moderate debt (C$17,144M versus C$46,796M equity), but returns collapse in oil downturns such as 2020's loss.

fcf.evidence: Over the twelve months to June 30, 2026, operating cash flow of C$17,813M less C$8,156M of capital spending left about C$9,657M of free cash flow, close to adjusted net earnings of C$10,526M.

b10.evidence: Retained earnings rose to C$32,726M at end-2025 while the share price rose from about US$9 (split-adjusted) at the start of 2021 to US$54.12, more than matching the retained profits.

safety.evidence: At about 13.7 times trailing earnings, 3.4 times book value and above the average analyst target, the price leaves no margin of safety against a fall in oil prices.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of about 11.6 looks reasonable for a low-cost producer, but it rests on 2026 oil prices and consensus revenue falls from C$48.6B in 2026 to C$42.9B in 2027.

mu5.evidence: Long-life reserves and moderate debt make failure unlikely, but oil-price collapses, carbon policy, pipeline access, tariffs and the energy transition are several ways to lose value.

reinvest.evidence: Debottlenecking and oil sands expansions (Jackpine 150,000 bbl/d, Pike 2 70,000 bbl/d) offer reinvestment, but they are on hold pending government agreements and most cash is returned to shareholders.

ly2.evidence: It is a clear cyclical: earnings track oil prices, with a loss in 2020 and record quarterly results in Q2 2026 when WTI averaged US$92.85.

ly3.evidence: A trailing P/E of about 13.7 is well above expected earnings growth, as consensus adjusted EPS falls about 10% from C$6.10 in 2026 to C$5.48 in 2027.

runway.evidence: Its 40-year proved plus probable reserve life supports output for decades, but sales growth depends on oil prices and slow volume growth, not new places or products.

ly7.evidence: The company is shrinking its share count (C$1,449M of buybacks in 2025, about 30.7 million shares repurchased in 2026 to August 5), but no notable open-market insider buying was found.

ly8.evidence: It is a widely followed large-cap covered by 23 analysts and about 81% owned by institutions.

fi2.evidence: Management plans new capacity as fields mature (Pike 1 pads, Jackfish debottlenecking, Horizon NRUTT project adding about 6,300 bbl/d in 2027), but these are more oil volumes, not new products.

fi3.evidence: Its technology work (e.g. paraffinic froth treatment and in-pit extraction studies, Oil Sands Alliance collaboration) has helped lower costs, but it does not report meaningful R&D spending.

fi4.evidence: It sells commodities at benchmark prices through marketing teams; there is no special selling advantage.

longterm.evidence: Management favours long-life, low-decline assets (about 73% of proved reserves) and pauses expansions until policy is secure, prioritising durable value over short-term volume.

gr1.evidence: It has a market value of about US$112 billion and produced 1,570,757 BOE/d in 2025.

ni10.evidence: Its filings show net losses of C$637M in 2015, C$204M in 2016 (Q4 2016 results release, Form 6-K, March 2017) and C$435M in 2020 (FY2022 Form 40-F).

gr4.evidence: The company reports 26 consecutive years of dividend growth through 2026, at a 20% compound annual rate.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS went from a loss of C$(0.58) in 2015 (pre-split; Q4 2016 results release, Form 6-K, March 2017) to C$5.16 in 2025 (FY2025 Form 40-F), far more than a one-third gain.

gr6.evidence: At about C$77.23 per share it trades near 19.7 times its three-year average diluted EPS of C$3.92 (2023-2025).

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 13.7 times P/B of about 3.4 gives roughly 47, about double Graham's 22.5 limit.

th1.evidence: It has no proprietary technology ten times better than rivals; Suncor and Imperial use similar mining and in situ methods.

timing.evidence: 2026 timing favours it with high oil prices from Middle East supply disruptions, but long-term oil demand timing is uncertain.

th3.evidence: It grew by acquiring and developing assets in a large existing market, not by dominating a small new one.

team.evidence: Executive Chair Murray Edwards has guided the company since 1988 into Canada's largest producer, and President Scott Stauth is a 28-year operations veteran who has raised guidance twice in 2026.
